§9.2.9 Split Tables Sharing a Header

📄 Page rule — applied from the page alone

tables-split-tables-sharing-a-header · tables boundaries headers proposed-rule

✅ Normative

Fragments that share a header row or a label column printed only once MUST be rendered as one table. The missing header is the proof that the second fragment was never meant to stand alone.

A grid is sometimes printed as two or more visually separated fragments — a gap, a page-design break, a divider — with the header row or the label column printed once and not repeated in the second fragment. Read on its own, the second fragment is unreadable without the header above it, so it is not a separate table. Emitting it as a separate headerless table, or dropping it, loses the meaning of every value in it (never drop).

Printed:   | Age | Rate M | Rate F |     ← header printed once
           | 25  | 1.10   | 1.05   |

              (visual gap / band)

           | 45  | 1.42   | 1.31   |     ← no header repeated: same table
           | 55  | 1.80   | 1.66   |

This is the mirror of the repeated-header test in Repeated Headers and Title Bands§9.2.7: a repeated header starts a new table, an unrepeated one continues the current one. Between them, header repetition is the single boundary signal on a page, read before gaps, rules or bands.

✅ Sample — 3samehead

The Count / % of Count / Premium / % of Premium header row is printed once and shared by three consecutive cohort blocks below it. None of the blocks below can be read on its own, so the page is one table with each cohort label as a band row.

Two cases that need judgement

Something sits in the gap. A band row, a caption or a paragraph between the fragments does not automatically break the table. The fragments MUST be merged as long as the second one still depends on the header above it; a heading printed in the gap becomes a band row inside the one table.

The shared piece is the label column. Side-by-side fragments with the row labels printed once on the left and value blocks separated by a gutter follow the same test: the value blocks cannot be read without those labels, so they MUST be rendered as one table. Every printed value MUST be kept, with the blocks placed as further columns of the labelled table.

✅ Sample — one label column, two value blocks

A quarterly summary printed as one row-label column on the left — Revenue, Gross profit, Selling, general and administrative expenses, EBIT, Non-controlling interests, Net income — feeding two separately boxed value blocks: C$ millions and (% of revenue), each with its own Q2 2025 / Q2 2024 header pair.

The right-hand block has no row labels of its own. Read on its own it is ten unnamed values, which is the proof that the two fragments were never meant to stand apart. The same structure is printed again below for the year-to-date figures, with its header rows repeated, so that block is a second table.

The blocks do not share a header row: each has its own. It is the label column that is printed once — the mirror sub-case. The em-dashes in the Non-controlling interests rows are values, not blanks (Marks and Symbols in Cells§9.6.6), and (% of revenue) is a units line in the header (Units Row§9.3.5). The empty gutter between the blocks is not a column (Gutter Columns§9.4.1).
